headline: 54 Bangladeshis died in Russia-Ukraine war after going for jobs; families left in despair
summary: Many Bangladeshis seeking better jobs in Russia have been allegedly sent to the Ukraine war front, with at least 54 reported dead over three years. Families face immense debt and uncertainty as bodies are not returned.
details: Abdullah Al Mamun from Lalmonirhat went to Russia for a better job but ended up in a war camp. The day before deployment, he called his brother, saying, "They are sending me to war; we might not meet again in this world. If not here, we will meet on the Day of Judgment."

Mamun's father confirmed losing contact after his son was sent to war. A friend later informed the family of Mamun's death, leading to a symbolic funeral where only prayers were offered due to uncertainty. Five months on, Mamun's debt-ridden family, including his wife and one-year-old son, faces a bleak future.

Mamun was among 30 Bangladeshis who traveled to Russia on May 7, lured by promises of high-paying jobs. After 21 days of training, they were divided into groups and sent to the war front, with many reportedly dying around June 12-13. Two individuals, Adnan Hossain and Rajon Hossain, were hospitalized but escaped and returned to Bangladesh, providing crucial information about the deaths.

This incident highlights a growing trend where Bangladeshis seeking jobs in Russia are deceived and end up in the Russia-Ukraine war. Prothom Alo reports at least 54 deaths over the past three years. Russia reportedly does not disclose information about Bangladeshi casualties or repatriate bodies, often listing them as missing, which families interpret as death.

Adnan Hossain, one of the returnees, suffered shrapnel wounds, underwent three surgeries, and spent two months in a Moscow hospital before escaping to the embassy and returning to Bangladesh. He stated that bodies of foreign combatants are typically not recovered and are left on the battlefield.

The Bangladesh Embassy in Russia has repeatedly objected to recruiting agencies sending workers without proper verification. A letter to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare detailed how agencies like Jabal-e Noor, RS International, and TS Overseas sent 30 workers, despite the embassy not verifying their permits, leading to their deployment to the war zone.

The Foreign Ministry is engaging with Russia, which has informed the embassy about 40 missing or deceased Bangladeshis, though without distinguishing between the two. Compensation claims for war victims are complex, requiring heirs to meet stringent conditions, and bodies are not recovered.

Bangladesh's Ambassador to Russia, Md. Nazrul Islam, stated that over 90% of workers voluntarily joined the war, with Russia possessing written proof. He confirmed that Russian authorities are not handing over bodies, preventing their repatriation.

International organizations, including Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds, reported 34 Bangladeshi deaths by March. The Special Response Battalion (SRB) also confirmed at least 20 deaths among 30 Bangladeshis sent to war in June. Families report that agencies promised responsibility but failed to provide proof of death or recovery of bodies.

headline_marked: [[Bijoya Dashami marks the formal end]] of this year's Sharadiya Durga Puja celebrations
headline: Bijoya Dashami marks the formal end of this year's Sharadiya Durga Puja celebrations
summary: Devotees bid farewell to Goddess Durga with final offerings, Sindur Khela, and Darpan Bisarjan, culminating in idol immersion later today.
details: Today marks Bijoya Dashami, the auspicious day that formally concludes this year's five-day Sharadiya Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community.
Rituals for Bijoya Dashami include 'Bihi Puja' and 'Darpan Bisarjan' (mirror immersion) in the morning at various mandaps. Devotees offer their final prayers and bid farewell to Goddess Durga.
From noon, the preparations for 'Sindur Khela' (smearing vermilion) and 'Pratima Bhasan' (idol immersion) processions will commence. These vibrant processions will head towards immersion ghats.

The five-day festival officially concludes with the symbolic immersion of the idols into water bodies. Strict security measures have been implemented to ensure all arrangements for Dashami conclude peacefully.
According to Sanatan scriptures, it is believed that Goddess Durga will return to Kailash on a boat this year, signifying a specific outcome for the year ahead.
caption:
Today is Bijoya Dashami, the final day of the five-day Sharadiya Durga Puja, marking the goddess's return.

Today marks Bijoya Dashami, the auspicious day that formally concludes this year's five-day Sharadiya Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community.

Rituals for Bijoya Dashami include 'Bihi Puja' and 'Darpan Bisarjan' (mirror immersion) in the morning at various mandaps. Devotees offer their final prayers and bid farewell to Goddess Durga.

From noon, the preparations for 'Sindur Khela' (smearing vermilion) and 'Pratima Bhasan' (idol immersion) processions will commence. These vibrant processions will head towards immersion ghats.

The five-day festival officially concludes with the symbolic immersion of the idols into water bodies. Strict security measures have been implemented to ensure all arrangements for Dashami conclude peacefully.

According to Sanatan scriptures, it is believed that Goddess Durga will return to Kailash on a boat this year, signifying a specific outcome for the year ahead.
